articles.era: 1995 Type I control using current combat rules
articles.matchup: The Deck against red-green creature aggression
articles.title: The Apes were ready, but the path was closed
articles.intro: A battlefield full of ground creatures can cease to be an attacking force without any of them taking damage. Moat is a four-mana rule about who can declare an attack, not a removal spell.
articles.lesson: Moat forbids creatures without flying from attacking while the enchantment remains on the battlefield. It does not forbid them from blocking and does not stop flying attackers, direct damage or any attacks made before it resolved.
articles.origin: Jeff A. Menges illustrated Moat for Legends in June 1994. The white enchantment is a continuing restriction on attack declarations, not a one-time Fog. Control shells such as the published Brian Weissman list could exploit this while retaining a flying win condition.
articles.technical: The attack restriction is checked as attackers are declared. If a defending player destroys Moat before attackers are declared, ground creatures may attack; if Moat remains, no amount of later combat-damage modification lets them join combat. Serra Angel can still attack because it has flying.
articles.history: The Brian Weissman — The Deck archival list includes Moat, Serra Angel, Counterspell and Disenchant. This shows a concrete white-blue control context but is not a source for the invented attack described in the reconstruction.
articles.story: My [[Moat]] had survived a full turn, and the three [[Kird Ape]]s opposite me still waited beside their [[Taiga]]. During my opponent's main phase, they cast [[Disenchant]] to clear the way. I tapped two [[Island]]s for [[Counterspell]] and watched Disenchant go to the graveyard. When combat began, the Apes could not be declared as attackers; they lacked flying. My [[Serra Angel]] was ready to attack on the following turn. The creature line across the table was still alive, but I was no longer counting its power as damage this combat.
articles.review: Documentary reference deck contains Moat, Serra Angel, Counterspell and Disenchant; opposing Kird Apes/Taiga are hypothetical. Counterspell uses two Islands for UU. Moat restricts attack declarations of nonfliers; it does not destroy or prevent combat damage.

articles.title: A Bolt paid for, then countered
articles.intro: A one-mana Lightning Bolt may be cast successfully and still never resolve: Nether Void creates a separate triggered counter unless the spell's caster can pay another three mana.
articles.lesson: The trigger occurs after casting a spell, including one cast by Nether Void's controller; paying {3} is not a casting-cost increase. Activated abilities of lands such as Mishra's Factory are not spells and do not trigger it.
articles.origin: Harold McNeill illustrated Nether Void for Legends in 1994. Its world-enchantment frame conveys a battlefield rule that changes how spells resolve. The printed tax is universal, not a loophole for its controller.
articles.technical: After Lightning Bolt has been cast for {R}, Nether Void puts a counter-unless-pay-{3} trigger above it. An opponent left with only two mana sources cannot pay the additional three on resolution. Counterspell-style permission and abilities operate on different layers; Nether Void does not tax activated abilities.
articles.history: Reid Duke's documented Mono-Black Pox list contains Nether Void and Mishra's Factory, a concrete example of a deck able to operate around the spell trigger. This article's burn opponent and individual game sequence are editorial reconstructions, not attributed coverage.
articles.story: My [[Nether Void]] was already on the battlefield when my opponent pointed [[Lightning Bolt]] at me. They tapped a [[Mountain]] for its red casting cost, leaving only two untapped mana-producing lands. Nether Void then triggered above Bolt on the stack. I asked whether they could pay another three; they could not. The trigger countered Bolt before it dealt damage. On my following turn I used [[Mishra's Factory]] as a creature threat. Animating the Factory was an activated ability, not casting a spell, so Nether Void offered no extra payment for that action.
articles.review: Opponent uses Mountain for red Bolt casting cost; trigger demands three additional mana on resolution, two available cannot pay. Nether Void does not increase printed spell cost. Mishra's Factory animation is activated ability.

articles.era: 2011 Legacy adapted to modern combat rules
articles.matchup: Mono-Black Pox against black-white midrange creatures
articles.title: The creature they chose to lose
articles.intro: The Abyss is not a sweeper. On each player's upkeep it identifies a single nonartifact creature of the active player's choice and destroys that creature without allowing regeneration.
articles.lesson: The Abyss controller controls its triggered ability, while the active player chooses which of their own nonartifact creatures is targeted. The trigger does not sacrifice anything and it cannot target an artifact creature.
articles.origin: Pete Venters illustrated The Abyss for Legends in June 1994. The world enchantment is compulsory attrition, but its one-creature-per-upkeep pacing leaves meaningful choices rather than emptying both sides on entry.
articles.technical: At the beginning of an upkeep, The Abyss targets a nonartifact creature chosen by that active player among their creatures. The chosen creature is destroyed and cannot regenerate. The active player does not choose a creature controlled by the enchantment's owner; an indestructible target would survive destruction.
articles.history: Reid Duke's 2011 Mono-Black Pox archive includes The Abyss as a particular prison option. The present vignette uses that deck's black-control context without claiming that Duke played the described game.
articles.story: At the start of my opponent's upkeep, [[The Abyss]] triggered with two of their creatures still on the battlefield: [[Black Knight]] and [[Hypnotic Specter]]. They chose the Knight as the target. I controlled the enchantment's ability, but I did not get to select their loss. When the trigger resolved, Black Knight was destroyed, not sacrificed, and regeneration was not available. My [[Mishra's Factory]] remained an ordinary land, not a creature, so there was no eligible target on my side for the next upkeep. Their Specter survived this turn and still threatened another attack.
articles.review: Abyss trigger controlled by enchantment controller, target chosen by active player among their own nonartifact creatures. One chosen Black Knight destroyed without regeneration; not a sacrifice; unanimated Factory remains noncreature.

articles.deck: Michael Loconto — Pro Tour New York 1996
articles.era: 1996 Standard representative play using current trigger wording
articles.title: One land behind, three Plains ahead in hand
articles.intro: Land Tax makes a player who controls fewer lands capable of collecting up to three basics during upkeep. The reward is cards in hand, not lands on the battlefield or free land drops.
articles.lesson: Land Tax has an intervening-if trigger: a rival must control more lands both as upkeep begins and when the trigger resolves. It searches for up to three basic lands and puts them into hand, without granting any additional land play.
articles.origin: Brian Snoddy's original Land Tax appeared in Legends in 1994. The white enchantment rewarded trailing in land count, creating a deck-building incentive different from ordinary acceleration.
articles.technical: A one-Plains controller facing two Islands has the required inequality at upkeep. Searching for three Plains changes their hand, not battlefield land count. Playing a second Plains later may shut off the next upkeep trigger if both players then have two lands.
articles.history: Michael Loconto's 1996 Pro Tour New York winning list contains Land Tax alongside Swords to Plowshares and white-blue control spells. The invented hand and land sequence here is illustrative rather than a match report.
articles.story: My [[Plains]] was the only land I controlled when my opponent untapped their two [[Island]]s. On my next upkeep, [[Land Tax]] saw their two lands against my one and triggered. Neither land count changed before resolution. I searched for three basic Plains, revealed them, put them into my hand, and shuffled. None entered the battlefield. Later in my main phase, I played my one land for the turn, then kept [[Swords to Plowshares]] ready for a creature. We now had two lands apiece, so another Tax trigger was not guaranteed on my following upkeep.
articles.review: 1 Plains versus 2 Islands at beginning of upkeep and resolution permits 3 basic Plains to hand. Later one regular land play makes land counts equal. No extra land play; deck contains Swords to Plowshares.

articles.title: I kept two cards and paid four life
articles.intro: Sylvan Library turns a draw step into three new cards to consider and a choice between putting drawn cards back or paying four life apiece to keep extras.
articles.lesson: The player draws a normal card first, may draw two additional cards with the Library trigger, then chooses two cards drawn this turn. For each chosen card they either pay four life or put it back on top. It is not three extra cards and it is not a selection from arbitrary old cards.
articles.origin: Harold McNeill illustrated Sylvan Library for Legends in June 1994. The green enchantment exchanges life and information for repeated card selection, an unusual source of patient advantage.
articles.technical: With no other draws earlier this turn, the relevant drawn set comprises the normal draw and two Library draws. Returning one of the chosen two and paying four life for the other leaves two of the three new cards in hand and changes a starting life total of 12 to 8. Future shuffle effects may alter the known next draw.
articles.history: Henry Stern's 1995 Vice Age runner-up list includes Sylvan Library along with burn and Black Vise pressure. The new scene is a representative read-time accounting exercise, not a 1995 match transcript.
articles.story: My opponent had a full hand across the table when I started the draw step at twelve life with [[Sylvan Library]] in play. I drew my normal card, then chose to draw two more with the Library trigger. All three were distinct from the cards I had held at the start of the turn. I selected two of the newly drawn cards: one went back on top of my library, and I paid four life to keep the other. My life total fell to eight. I still had [[Lightning Bolt]] and [[Black Vise]] as part of my plan, but the Library had bought only one extra card, not three.
articles.review: Normal draw 1 plus optional 2 Library draws = 3 this turn. Choose two among those; put one back and pay four life for other. Life 12->8; two of three cards remain, exactly one extra kept. Other cited cards documented in Vice Age.

articles.era: 1994 World Championship using modern haste keyword
articles.title: The new Elf could tap immediately
articles.intro: Concordant Crossroads grants haste to every creature, including creatures just summoned by the opponent. Its one-green-mana enchantment can accelerate a play or expose a whole plan.
articles.lesson: Haste allows a newly controlled creature to attack and activate its own tap-symbol abilities despite the normal summoning-sickness restriction. Crossroads grants the keyword to all creatures, not just its controller's, and does not itself untap anything.
articles.origin: Amy Weber's Concordant Crossroads debuted in Legends in June 1994 as a world enchantment. It offered green a battlefield-wide haste permission long before the keyword was printed in the modern way.
articles.technical: Tap a Forest for Llanowar Elves, then a second Forest for Concordant Crossroads. The Elves has haste and can tap for green immediately. That is one extra mana from a new creature rather than an extra land drop; any opponent's creatures also gain haste.
articles.history: The archive's Mark's Little Deck records Concordant Crossroads and Llanowar Elves as an early 1994 blue-green tempo strategy. The turn-by-turn mana sequence is a representative reconstruction, not attributed game coverage.
articles.story: The first [[Forest]] cast my [[Llanowar Elves]] during my main phase, and the new Elf could not yet tap for mana. I tapped my second Forest to cast [[Concordant Crossroads]] for one green. The enchantment resolved; it gave every creature haste, including the Elf I had just played. I tapped that Elf for one green mana, leaving both lands tapped. My opponent's [[Kird Ape]] would receive haste too if it entered on their next turn, so passing without using the extra mana had a real cost. The enchantment did not create another land drop.
articles.review: Two Forests each produce green for Elves and Crossroads. Newly controlled Elf obtains haste and may tap for {G} on the same turn; Crossroads symmetric. Opposing Kird Ape is fictional.

articles.era: 1994 Old School model using modern rules
articles.matchup: Nested Draw Control against white-green creature midrange
articles.title: Passing once did not end the spell
articles.intro: Eureka is a four-mana invitation to both players to put permanents from their hands onto the battlefield. One pass does not necessarily finish the sequence.
articles.lesson: Players take turns choosing permanents; a player who declines a turn can still place one later if the process continues. The sequence ends only after all players consecutively decline to put a card onto the battlefield, and cards put onto the battlefield are not cast.
articles.origin: Kaja Foglio illustrated Eureka for Legends in June 1994. The green sorcery compressed many turns of spending mana into one mutually visible resolution, creating reward for the best hand and danger from the opponent's.
articles.technical: During resolution both players may put permanent cards onto the battlefield in turn. The first pass is not a permanent waiver. Enters-the-battlefield triggers wait until the spell finishes resolving before joining the stack; cast triggers do not fire for these objects.
articles.history: Groundhog Day — Nested Draw Control is explicitly a curated Old School example, not a verified event registration. The article uses it as a card-pool illustration only; no result or player testimony is attributed to it.
articles.story: I resolved [[Eureka]] with [[Mirror Universe]] and [[Sylvan Library]] in my hand. On my first opportunity I put Mirror Universe onto the battlefield. My opponent chose [[Serra Angel]]. I followed with Sylvan Library; my opponent declined their next opportunity. I passed on the next choice too, but we had not yet finished the spell just because one player had passed. When my opponent's turn to choose arrived again, they could still put another permanent from hand onto the battlefield. None of these permanents was cast; any enters-the-battlefield triggers waited until Eureka finished resolving.
articles.review: Eureka alternates choices, does not end after one pass, cards are put onto battlefield rather than cast, triggers wait until resolution. Groundhog Day reference curated, opponent Serra Angel hypothetical. Historical date 1994 Old School style not claimed match.

articles.era: 2023 Old School using current combat and activated-ability rules
articles.matchup: U/G Control against blue-white flying creature aggression
articles.title: The second attacker met the same Maze
articles.intro: Candelabra of Tawnos converts mana into land untaps. The classic artifact does not produce mana itself; it offers a new use for an already valuable utility land.
articles.lesson: {X}, {T} targets exactly X lands and untaps them when the activated ability resolves. It is not a mana ability, can target untapped lands, and may be disrupted on the stack. Candelabra became banned in Legacy on June 29, 2026.
articles.origin: Douglas Shuler illustrated Candelabra of Tawnos for Antiquities in March 1994. Its deceptively short activated ability became dangerous whenever lands produced unusually high returns or repeatable tactical effects.
articles.technical: One untapped Sol Ring supplies two colorless mana. Spending one for Candelabra with X=1 untaps a previously tapped Maze of Ith; the second can face another attacker. Candelabra itself is now tapped, so the maneuver is not limitless without a separate untap engine.
articles.history: The Odd Anders Kjostvedt U/G Control archive records Candelabra and Maze together in Old School. Separately, Wizards of the Coast banned Candelabra in Legacy effective June 29, 2026, citing problematic combo applications. Former Legacy High Tide and 2026 Tron lists are historical evidence, not current legal Legacy recommendations.
articles.story: My opponent attacked with [[Serra Angel]] and [[Air Elemental]]. I had [[Maze of Ith]] and [[Candelabra of Tawnos]] untapped, with [[Sol Ring]] ready. Before combat damage, I tapped Maze targeting the Angel, preventing its combat damage. Then I tapped Sol Ring for two colorless mana and spent one on Candelabra with X equal to one, targeting my tapped Maze. The ability resolved and untapped Maze. I tapped Maze again targeting the Air Elemental. Neither flyer dealt combat damage, while one colorless mana remained floating. Candelabra was tapped now; it had not generated any mana.
articles.review: 2023 Kjostvedt U/G list includes Candelabra, Maze and Sol Ring; flyers are fictional. Two distinct Maze activations made possible by X=1 Candelabra costing one of Sol Ring's two colorless, then untapping Maze. Both attackers remained attacking. Legacy legal claim must use June 29, 2026 ban.

articles.era: 1994 Old School model with current Oracle wording
articles.matchup: Nested Draw Control against mono-blue control
articles.title: Nothing was sacrificed until the spell resolved
articles.intro: Transmute Artifact is a tutor with a consequential timing detail: its artifact sacrifice happens when the sorcery resolves, not when the spell is cast. Countering it can prevent any artifact from being sacrificed.
articles.lesson: Casting costs {U}{U} without sacrificing anything. On resolution its controller sacrifices one artifact, searches for another, and either puts it directly onto the battlefield or pays the mana-value difference. A found higher-value artifact goes to the graveyard if that difference is not paid.
articles.origin: Anson Maddocks illustrated Transmute Artifact for Antiquities in March 1994. The early blue tutor carries both a search effect and a potential mana-value payment; modern Oracle clarification moved the sacrifice timing to resolution rather than an added cost.
articles.technical: With Sol Ring (mana value one) on the battlefield, a resolved Transmute Artifact can sacrifice it and find Mana Vault (also mana value one) without an additional payment. If the search instead finds a more expensive artifact, the difference is paid during resolution; that is not part of the spell's casting cost.
articles.history: The archived Groundhog Day Nested Draw Control list is explicitly a curated example, not a tournament registration. Its Sol Ring and Mana Vault demonstrate a possible conversion; no result or named player's game is invented.
articles.story: Two blue sources, [[Tundra]] and [[Tropical Island]], paid for my [[Transmute Artifact]]. I left [[Sol Ring]] on the battlefield while the sorcery waited on the stack. My opponent could have countered it without forcing a sacrifice, but they let it resolve. Only then did I sacrifice Sol Ring and search my library for [[Mana Vault]], another artifact with mana value one. Vault entered the battlefield without an additional payment, and I shuffled. I had not paid a sacrifice cost while casting the spell, and Vault had entered without being cast, so there was no separate artifact spell on the stack.
articles.review: Original 1994 era represented with modern Oracle wording; Transmute Artifact sacrifice is an EFFECT of spell resolution, not an additional cost; Counterspell before resolution leaves original artifact intact. Sacrifice MV1 Sol Ring, find MV1 Mana Vault, no difference; Tundra and Tropical Island each blue pay UU. Groundhog Day archive curated.

articles.deck: Power Artifact — Basalt Monolith study deck
articles.era: 2000-era casual Type I card pool using 2006+ Oracle rules
articles.matchup: Blue artifact combo against blue-black control
articles.title: The Monolith paid three and untapped for one
articles.intro: Power Artifact turns the generic mana in artifact activation costs into a combo equation. Enchant Basalt Monolith: its three-mana untap cost drops to one, while tapping the Monolith still produces three colorless.
articles.lesson: The Aura reduces the generic portion of the enchanted artifact's activated-ability costs by {2}, not below one mana when a mana payment is present. It does not discount casting costs, colored mana, tap costs or mana abilities that already cost zero.
articles.origin: Douglas Shuler illustrated Power Artifact for Antiquities in March 1994. The combination with Basalt Monolith became a classic cost-reduction example; Wizards later specifically removed power-level errata restricting Basalt Monolith's self-untap in July 2006.
articles.technical: Tap Basalt Monolith for {C}{C}{C}; with Power Artifact attached, pay one generic to untap it, retaining two floating. Repeating can build arbitrarily large colorless mana. A payoff such as Stroke of Genius still needs its colored blue requirement, and destroying the Aura or artifact during a priority window ends the loop.
articles.history: Wizards of the Coast documented Power Artifact + Grim Monolith as an infinite-mana combo in its 2003 Top 50 Blue Cards retrospective, and described removing Basalt Monolith's self-untap restriction in 2006. The added 60-card deck is a curated period-plausible rules study, not any player registration or tournament result.
articles.story: My [[Basalt Monolith]] had been in play since the previous turn when I tapped two [[Island]]s to cast [[Power Artifact]] on it. The Aura resolved. I tapped Monolith for three colorless mana, spent one to activate its discounted untap ability, and kept two floating. I untapped Monolith and tapped it for three more. Repeating that exchange could build as much colorless mana as I needed, but [[Stroke of Genius]] would still require blue mana from another source. I watched my opponent's untapped [[Underground Sea]]: removing the Aura at the right moment could leave the Monolith unable to continue.
articles.review: Power Artifact costs UU paid by two Islands, enchants prior Basalt Monolith. Its {3} untap activated cost reduced by {2} to {1}, maintaining one-mana floor; tapped Monolith adds three colorless, net +2 per cycle. Opposing Underground Sea fictional. Deck is explicitly curated, not a historical 60-card tournament registration.
